newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Norilsk may top 97 nickel output table, up exports.
newsitem.headline: Norilsk may top 97 nickel output table, up exports.

text.p: Russia's troubled Norilsk Nickel metals group may become the world's number one nickel producer this year with its ambitious output plans, but its financial crisis raises questions over how it might achieve such a feat.
RAO Norilsky Nikel, which accounts for around 85 percent of Russian nickel output, plans to expand output of the metal by 20 percent in 1997 to 213,000 tonnes from 177,185 in 1996.
Analysts said Norilsk had enough spare capacity to achieve its aim. But they wondered if it had the finances.

"Estimated capacity utilisation in 1996 was 68 percent," said Dmitry Chernak, metals analyst at ING-Barings in Moscow. "Not all installed capacity could be immediately utilised, but it could well reach 80 percent fairly quickly."
He pegged full annual nickel production capacity at the Norilsk group at 265,000 tonnes.
Some analysts doubted the target could be hit in a year.

"It is quite possible they will produce more, but 213,000 tonnes I think is too much -- I am looking at a production number of 200,000 tonnes in 1997," said Fidelis Madavo, nickel specialist at CRU International in London.

Norilsk announced last month it was showing signs of bankruptcy, so severe were its 1996 consolidated losses. Its production operations are still profitable, but enormous social costs have weighed the company down.
The firm plans to hive off social obligations to municipal budgets, freeing up cash to invest in expanding output. But some analysts said the process would take longer than a year.
"We are talking about a big operation here," Madavo said.
Russian demand for nickel, used mainly in stainless steel manufacture, is unlikely to pick up much this year, raising the spectre of a flood of Russian material on to world markets.
"Nickel exports will be strong this year," said Chernak.
Traders in Europe are already reporting plentiful supply from the Norilsk metals group -- producer of about one fifth of the world's nickel.
"A lot of the big physical trading companies are saying that quite a bit of Russian material is already floating around in Europe," Madavo said.
If the flow from Russia picks up as some expect, the implications for nickel prices could be serious.
Norilsk's expansion plans and rising exports in 1996, as well as official data for nickel exports in 1997, have sent analysts scurrying to their spreadsheets to revise price forecasts down.
Madavo said he had revised his average nickel price forecast down to $3.50-3.55 per pound on a cash basis in 1997 from just over $3.60 previously.

"Last year Russia exported a lot more than we originally thought, with Norilsk announcing a 20 percent increase on 1995," Madavo said. "If you factor this in, it means you had a small surplus last year, which changes the outlook somewhat."
Even more alarming than rising output and exports at Norilsk were data from the State Statistics Committee showing first quarter Russian nickel exports up 48 percent year-on-year to 50,300 tonnes.
"You have to start taking all of this seriously," said one London-based nickel analyst.
If the customs committee data are accurate, and if exports continue at the same rate throughout 1997, prices could head for a downward spiral, analysts say.
"If exports continued at the same rate as officially set in the first quarter, that would kill this market. It would throw it into a serious surplus," said Madavo.
And were Norilsk to come anywhere close to fulfilling its expansion plan, it would become the world's number one producer of finished nickel in 1997, analysts said.
Inco of Canada, which in 1996 held the number one spot, plans to produce just over 195,455 tonnes in 1997.

Inco would remain the world's top supplier, however, with plans to deliver over 227,000 tonnes to customers this year, including purchases from London Metal Exchange (LME) stocks and other nickel producers.
The pressure on Norilsk, which ran up huge financial losses in 1996, to export metals to hard currency buyers will be great.
But now that Norilsk has a sole export agent, Interrosimpex, the company's sensitivity to LME prices could strengthen.
"Norilsk's expansion plans partly depend on where metal prices are," Chernak said.
